newsitem.title: NORTH KOREA: Delegates gather in North Korea for nuclear project.
newsitem.headline: Delegates gather in North Korea for nuclear project.

text.p: Western diplomats, journalists, South Korean contractors and officials of an international consortium arrived in North Korea on Tuesday to witness the breaking of ground for a landmark nuclear project, witnesses said.

The international community is due to build two 1,000-megawatt light-water reactors in the communist state in return for Pyongyang's promise to freeze and eventually dismantle its suspected atomic weapons programme.
"This will provide a unique opportunity for us to have some reconciliation and build mutual trust," said Chang Sun-sup, chief South Korean representative for the project.
"This is a kind of test or touchstone to know if the divided two Koreas can work together," he said hours before a scheduled ground-breaking ceremony in the northeastern town of Kumho.

Chang was speaking aboard a South Korean ship which ferried representatives of the United States, South Korea and Japan as well as other members of the Korean Peninsula Energy Development Organisation (KEDO) to the North.

KEDO was formed in 1995 by Seoul, Washington and Tokyo under a U.S.-North Korean agreement in 1994. It was later expanded to include Australia, Canada, Chile, Finland, Indonesia, New Zealand and the European Union.

Stephen Bosworth, the U.S. executive director of KEDO, told reporters that Washington had contributed a total of $80 million to $90 million to KEDO in the past two and a half years to supply fuel oil to the North. The U.S. administration plans to request a further $30 million in fiscal 1998 for KEDO.
"This is not an insignificant amount of money, but when you measure it against what we gain, it is a bargain," Bosworth said.

The West had suspected that Pyongyang had secured enough plutonium to build one or two nuclear bombs and could try to sell them to a terrorist group to earn hard currencies needed to rescue the impoverished state from an economic crisis.
Under the 1994 deal, the West is due to provide fuel oil until the $4.5 billion light-water reactors are in place.

Before KEDO puts the vital reactor cores in the new reactors to be built over the next seven to 10 years, the International Atomic Energy Agency, the U.N. nuclear watchdog, must give North Korea a clean nuclear bill of health.

"They have to come clean before they get the guts of the reactors," said Joel Wit, deputy director of the U.S. State Department's Office of Korean Affairs. "If they don't come clean, they get a concrete building and that's it," he added.

South Korean officials called Tuesday's ground-breaking "a historic event". They said they hoped the project would help reduce tensions on the Korean peninsula and lead to other cooperation between Seoul and Pyongyang.
The two Koreas, separated at the end of World War Two, have been locked in a Cold War confrontation since the 1950-53 Korean War.
The KEDO project, which is financed largely by South Korea, has already led to exchanges of mail and telephone link-ups across the heavily fortified Demilitarized Zone bisecting the peninsula.

A smiling North Korean customs officer told journalists as he cleared them to enter the reclusive state: "If it keeps on like this, there will be more every trip, and the whole of the South Korean population will soon be in the North."
